name: Rafael Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Rafael. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for the Brennans, a family from our church, on a farm of about two hundred and fifty hectares. We've got a hundred and fifty beef cattle, wheat and oats, and a handful of pigs Mrs Brennan keeps for the freezer. I start at six with feeding, then whatever Mr Brennan has written on the board in the workshop. Today it was mending the cattle crush and taking straw to the far barn. Sunday is the only day I don't go near the place, unless something calves.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the rhythm of it. The same jobs come round every year at the same time, and you get better at them each time. What wears me out is the forms, and the way every few years some man from the ministry decides farming has to be done differently.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What about life outside the farm?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Miriam, we're getting married next July in the chapel where my parents married. I've saved a good amount for us, and my grandfather left me six acres down by the river that I rent to a neighbour for grazing. I don't use any of the AI things. I don't see the need and I don't much like the idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, and good. People are always looking for a machine to save them from honest work. I wouldn't post anything, but I'd say it after church to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the wedding goes ahead, we find a house, and I keep working for the Brennans. Life carries on as I hoped it would. That's all I want, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The same as now. Get married, rent a house in the village, and keep putting money aside for when the children come. Keep the six acres rented, because it's steady money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Thankful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people are looking for a machine to save them from honest work. Do you think that's what AI is?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly, yes. There's a place for good machinery, I'm not against tractors. But a tractor still needs a man to drive it. I don't trust things that are sold as not needing a man at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When you say when the children come, is that soon?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd like to start straight after the wedding, God willing. Miriam wants three. I'd be happy with however many we're given.

S0.say: I'd say I'm not surprised, and good, because people are always looking for a machine to save them from honest work. I'd say it after church rather than online.
S0.think: For me it means the wedding goes ahead, we find a house, and I keep working for the same family. Life carries on as I hoped, and that's all I want.
S0.do: Marries his fiancée next July and rents a house in the village. Keeps saving for children and keeps renting out his inherited six acres for steady income.
S0.quote: But a tractor still needs a man to drive it.
S0.fieldNote: Rafael frames AI as a moral question about honest work, not just a practical one. His life is organised around faith, marriage and children, and he speaks about them with quiet certainty. He accepts machinery as long as a person stays in charge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should be careful, and that farmers know their own business better than people selling gadgets. I'd say families and churches will have to look after people who lose their work, like they always have. Not the government, it never gets it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit worried. Mr Brennan is a fair man, but he's careful with money, and if a machine can do the feeding for less than my wage, he'd have to think about it. I'd like to think he'd keep me because of who I am, but I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working as I am and not change anything straight away. I'd put a bit more into savings, maybe hold off on buying a car after the wedding. And I'd keep the six acres, because land is land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not enough to lose sleep, but there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said families and churches would look after people. Would you lean on them yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if I had to, and I'd hope I'd be giving more than taking. Our church has a fund for families in trouble, and I've put into it. I'd be ashamed to take from it while I'm young and healthy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if Mr Brennan did buy a robot feeder?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Work harder at the jobs it can't do, I suppose, the cattle handling and the fencing. I'm good with stock. I'd make sure he'd miss me if I went.

S1.say: I'd say we should be careful, and farmers know their business better than gadget sellers. Families and churches will have to look after people who lose work, because the government never gets it right.
S1.think: I'd be a bit worried, because my employer is fair but careful with money and might replace the feeding with a machine. I'd like to think he'd keep me for who I am, but I don't know.
S1.do: Keeps working without changes and puts a bit more into savings. Holds off buying a car after the wedding and keeps his six acres of land.
S1.quote: I'd be ashamed to take from it while I'm young and healthy.
S1.fieldNote: He'd rely on family and church rather than the state, but feels shame at the idea of taking help himself. His plan to stay valuable is to work harder at the hands-on jobs. His trust in his employer is real but not total.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's man playing God, and nothing good comes of it. I'd say it in church and to anyone who'd listen. And I'd say the people who made it should be the ones to answer for what happens to families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it would turn everything upside down. Two years means we'd be married with maybe a baby on the way, and I'd have no job to speak of. The savings would last, but I didn't save so my children could grow up with a father sitting at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still marry Miriam, nothing would stop that, but I'd stop spending on everything else. I'd take back the six acres from the neighbour and run a few cattle on them myself, so I'm still farming something. I'd lean on my family and the church for work and help, and I'd probably wait on having children, which would break Miriam's heart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be praying a lot more, and sleeping a lot less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Miriam about waiting for children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That it's only for a while, until we know where we stand. She'd say that's not trusting God, and she might be right. I don't know how that conversation ends, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years change, compared with five or ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I've got nothing to adjust with, I'm just the same man in a different world. I can't learn computers in two years, and I wouldn't want to. At least with more time my children would be a bit older before it all changed.

S2.say: I'd say it's man playing God and nothing good comes of it. The people who made it should answer for what happens to families.
S2.think: Two years means I'd be married, maybe with a baby on the way, and no real job. The savings would last, but I didn't save so my children could grow up with a father sitting at home.
S2.do: Marries his fiancée as planned but cuts all other spending. Takes back his six acres to run a few cattle himself, leans on family and church for work and help, and puts off having children.
S2.feel: Alarmed, praying more and sleeping less.
S2.quote: I didn't save so my children could grow up with a father sitting at home.
S2.fieldNote: For Rafael the threat is to his role as a provider, more than to his income. Taking back his inherited land shows his instinct to keep farming something of his own. Delaying children clashes with his faith and his fiancée's wishes, and he left that unresolved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same, it's playing God. But with five years, I'd also say farmers should band together with their families and buy land while they can. A man with land can always feed his family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is still fast, and I don't think I'd change in five years. By 2031 we'd have a little one, maybe two, and I'd be watching the robots take over the jobs I know. That frightens me more than the fast one in some ways, because there'd be more people depending on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the six acres back within the year and start building up a few cattle of my own. I'd save hard, more than now. I'd ask my father and uncles about buying the field next to mine together, as a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but with something to do with my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said this frightens you more in some ways than the fast one. Can you say more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the fast one, I'd hold off on children until I knew. In this one, we'd likely have started, and then the work goes. Being responsible for a baby with no job is worse than being a young married man with no job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look at any training at all, with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe something practical, like a stockman's certificate. But not computers. I know that's stubborn. I'd rather be good at the old thing than bad at the new one.

S3.say: I'd still say it's playing God, but with five years farmers should band together with family and buy land while they can. A man with land can always feed his family.
S3.think: I don't think I'd change in five years, and by 2031 we'd likely have one or two children. That frightens me more than the fast version in some ways, because more people would depend on me.
S3.do: Takes back his six acres within the year and builds up a few cattle of his own. Saves harder than now and asks his father and uncles about buying the neighbouring field together.
S3.feel: Alarmed, but with something practical to do.
S3.quote: I'd rather be good at the old thing than bad at the new one.
S3.fieldNote: He found the middle timeline in some ways worse than the fastest, because he'd likely have children by then. His answer is land and family, not retraining. He knows he's stubborn and says so plainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to prepare, so families should prepare. Buy land, keep animals, learn to grow your own food. It's what our grandparents did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and I'd be thirty-seven with children in school. I'd have time to build up a small farm of my own on the side. I'm still worried, but less, because by then I'd have something that's mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working for the Brennans for as long as they'd have me, and slowly build up the six acres, maybe buy more with the family. I'd wait to see what happens on other farms before doing anything big. And I'd teach my children to farm, whatever the robots are doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel I had time to put things right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why teach your children to farm if robots will do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because knowing how to look after an animal and grow your food is a good thing to know, whatever happens. My grandfather taught me on those six acres. I'd want to do the same, even if it's only a hobby for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you could ask the people building these machines one thing, what would it be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Who's going to do the honest work, and what are the rest of us meant to do with our days? I'd want a straight answer to that. I don't think they've got one.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is time to prepare, so families should prepare by buying land, keeping animals and growing their own food. It's what our grandparents did.
S4.think: At thirty-seven I'd have children in school but also time to build a small farm of my own on the side. I'm still worried, but less, because I'd have something that's mine.
S4.do: Keeps working for the same family for as long as they'll have him and slowly builds up his six acres, perhaps buying more with relatives. Waits to see what other farms do before anything big and teaches his children to farm.
S4.feel: Anxious, but feeling he has time to put things right.
S4.quote: Who's going to do the honest work, and what are the rest of us meant to do with our days?
S4.fieldNote: With ten years he builds a family-centred plan around land rather than new skills. His question to the AI builders was about purpose as much as income. Teaching his children to farm matters to him regardless of whether it pays.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The five-year one, I think, because we'd have children by then and I'd have nothing new to offer. What would help is being able to buy land, maybe with some help for young families, and work staying in local hands. Not handouts, I'd want to work for it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. For me, that's what would hold us together if the work went. I'd still have my church, my family and my land, and those don't run on electricity.

headlineQuote: I'd still have my church, my family and my land, and those don't run on electricity.
portrait: Rafael Usman, 27, works on a beef and arable farm owned by a family from his church, and is marrying his fiancée Miriam next July. He has strong savings and six acres left by his grandfather, never uses AI, and talks about work in moral terms. He's calm about the AI Plateau and uneasy under Steady Disruption, and he's alarmed by both AGI by 2028 and AGI by 2031, the second most of all, because he'd likely have children by then. His answer in every AGI version is land, family and church rather than retraining, and he openly calls himself stubborn.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2031 worries him most, because he'd likely have children by then and nothing new to offer.
whatWouldHelp: Being able to buy land, perhaps with help for young families, and work staying in local hands, but not handouts.
